title: Register pressure map and fused-op reorder playbook
content:
Purpose
- Short: capture an experimental playbook for measuring how register pressure interacts with fused-op ordering and attention kernel choice (FlashAttention vs paged vs simple fused kernels).
- Long: we suspect some tail latency and throughput regressions when a fused op ordering increases per-thread register allocation, pushing kernels into higher register-spill and lower wave occupancy. This doc collects reproducible steps, lightweight mapping techniques, examples of traces, and mitigations to try.

Background / why this matters
- Fused ops reduce global memory traffic and operator overhead but can increase per-thread live ranges. On Ampere/A100/Blackwell-like GPUs this can raise register allocation per thread, decreasing the number of active warps and reducing latency-hiding.
- We have intermittent throughput dropouts in mixed short/long seq workloads where the same model rolled back to a non-fused variant restored throughput. Need systematic investigation.

Hypotheses
1) Reordering q,k,v/bias add before or after an intermediate fused matmul+gelu changes compiler register assignments, increasing spills for some kernels.
2) Smaller sequence lengths (<= 64) with many concurrent contexts amplify occupancy sensitivity: fused ops that increase registers hurt small-seq throughput more.
3) FlashAttention tends to use fewer registers for attention math but fused QKV pipelines can still drive up per-thread pressure in certain fusion shapes.

High-level experiment plan
- Controlled microbench harness: single-op microbench with synthetic inputs (batch, seq_len, head_dim) swept.
- Compile three kernel variants (baseline unfused, fused-order-A, fused-order-B) and measure: cycles, achieved_occupancy, registers_per_thread, l1/shared reuse, global_mem_bw.
- Use NVPROF / Nsight Systems to capture per-kernel register_alloc and liveness where possible; fallback to cuobjdump/ptxinspect for static register count.
- Run end-to-end server traces with 95/99/99.9 p99 quantiles and correlate kernel-level occupancy changes.

Repro scripts (sketch)
- Build microbench: tools/microbench/attn_fused_harness.py
- Example run: python tools/microbench/attn_fused_harness.py --model=toy --bs=8 --seq=32 --head-dim=64 --variant=baseline --iters=5000
- Profiling: nv-nsight-cu-cli --metrics sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active --target-processes all --output baseline-32.nsys python ...
- Static inspection: cuobjdump -sass libkernels.so | grep -A4 "mov.u32 %r"  # crude, look for register spills in PTX/ASM

Microbench matrix to sweep
- batch sizes: 1, 4, 8, 16
- sequence lengths: 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256
- head dims: 32, 64, 96, 128
- fusion shapes: unfused, qkv-fused-then-matmul, qkv-then-bias-then-matmul, bias-then-qkv-fuse
- kernels: flash_attn_forward, paged_attn_kernel, fused_qkv_matmul

Key metrics to collect per-run (tabular CSV):
- variant, bs, seq, hd, kernel_name, time_ms, cycles, registers_per_thread, achieved_occupancy_pct, l1_hit_rate, gross_global_bw_GBps, p95_ms, p99_ms

Example observations (toy data from initial run)
- variant: qkv-fused-then-matmul; bs=8 seq=32 hd=64; kernel=fused_qkv_matmul
  - time_ms: 0.42, registers_per_thread: 64, occupancy: 33%, global_bw: 110 GB/s
- variant: unfused; same params
  - time_ms: 0.31, registers_per_thread: 44, occupancy: 60%, global_bw: 210 GB/s
- Note: fused variant higher latency despite lower global BW because occupancy dropped. Correlated with higher register count from cuobjdump.

Tracing notes: how to link kernel behavior to p99 tail
- Collect endpoint-level traces (X-Request-Id) with per-token durations and the list of kernels invoked.
- For each slow request, sample Nsight or nvprof around the time window (short trace capture to avoid overhead). Identify long-running kernels and their register counts.
- If slow tail maps to many small kernel invocations where occupancy < 40% and registers_per_thread > 60, mark as register-pressure-induced.

Compiler/driver interactions to be aware of
- PTX->SASS register allocation may differ across driver versions. Recompile kernels with a fixed CUDA/driver combo when comparing.
- Use -maxrregcount to force a register limit to observe performance cliffs (good experimental knob): e.g., nvcc -Xptxas -v -Xptxas -O3 -maxrregcount=48. Watch for spills causing increases in local memory traffic.

Quick check commands
- inspect registers (compiled cubin): cuobjdump --dump-sass libkernels.so | rg "reg_count|$kernel_name" -n
- Nsight metric example: sm__inst_executed.avg_per_cycle_active, smsp__thread_inst_executed.sum, sm__warps_active.avg
- small occupancy probe: python tools/occupancy_probe.py --kernel fused_qkv_matmul --bs 8 --seq 32

Potential mitigations to try (ordered)
1) Reorder fusion to reduce live range: break out short-lived temporaries so register allocator can reuse.
2) Add explicit memory spills for intermediate arrays when acceptable (trade compute for occupancy).
3) Reduce in-kernel unrolled loops or lower compile-time unroll factor for small seq shapes.
4) Token-aware routing: route low-seq traffic to variants compiled with low-maxrregcount to maximize occupancy.
5) Use FlashAttention for attention-heavy hotspots when it shows lower register footprint.

Small experiment checklist (immutable)
- Pin driver: CUDA 12.2 + driver 535.x during whole sweep.
- Ensure clocks: nvidia-smi -ac to set consistent clocks in lab.
- Disable power capping, isolate test GPU from other tenants.
- Capture per-kernel metrics for at least 1000 inferences to get stable percentiles.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Is the compiler assigning more registers because of specific PTX patterns produced by our fused op generator? Need PTX diffs.
- Can we automatically detect harmful fusions at build time by estimating the register delta?
- For multi-tenant Dedicated nodes, can we pick per-pool kernel variants based on observed seq distribution?

Draft timeline (2 sprints)
- Sprint 1 (2 weeks): build harness, sweep small matrix, collect CSVs, produce register maps for top 10 worst variants.
- Sprint 2 (2 weeks): try reorder/micro-refactor mitigations, push candidate kernel variants behind runtime feature flag, run end-to-end p99 comparisons.

Notes to self / TODOs
- Upload microbench harness to GH PR referenced above.
- Attach canonical CSV outputs and a simple plotting notebook in experiments/attach directory.
- Loop in Maya for shader-level inspection and Jonah for runtime routing changes.

Appendix: quick-reference observation from 2026-02-20 lab run
- GPU: A100-SXM4 80GB, CUDA 12.2, driver 535.54
- Workload: synthetic mix 70% seq<=32, 30% seq>=128, bs distribution heavy at 8.
- Result: switching to unfused qkv reduced p99 token latency from 18.4ms -> 12.1ms for the small-seq mix; average token cost increased modestly.

Contact / ownership
- Owner: Elena Martinez (eng-serving-runtime)
- Collabs: Ravi (kernel), Maya (profiling), Jonah (runtime)

End of playbook - this is a working doc. Keep notes short and append raw CSVs separately.
